concept.name: Deflation
concept.definition: A sustained general decline in the prices of goods and services, equivalently an increase in the purchasing power of money. It is typically associated with contracting money and credit or collapsing aggregate demand and is considered more dangerous than moderate inflation because it raises the real burden of debt and encourages delayed spending.
concept.intuition: When prices fall broadly, cash gains value just by sitting still, so consumers postpone purchases and borrowers must repay debts with more valuable money — a self-reinforcing drag on the economy.
concept.mechanics: Deflation shows up as a negative 12-month change in a price index (e.g., CPI below zero). Causes include falls in aggregate demand, contractions in money and credit (as in the 1930s U.S. bank failures), or strong productivity gains; policymakers counter it with rate cuts, asset purchases, and fiscal stimulus.
concept.formula: Deflation occurs when (CPI_t / CPI_{t-12} - 1) < 0, i.e., a negative inflation rate.
concept.failure_modes: As a concept it can mislead when driven by productivity or technology (good deflation) rather than demand collapse; debt-deflation dynamics described by Fisher apply mainly when falling prices coincide with high leverage.
concept.misconceptions: Cheaper prices are not always good: economy-wide deflation raises real debt burdens and real interest rates even at zero nominal rates, which is why central banks fight it as hard as inflation.
concept.example: The U.S. last experienced significant deflation in the early 1930s after widespread bank failures shrank the money supply; Japan suffered prolonged deflation in the 1990s.

citations.source: Investopedia — Deflation: Definition, Causes, and Impact
